title: Graphs of Exponential Functions
learningObjective: Graph exponential functions and determine the domain, range, and asymptotes.

faqs.question: What does the basic graph of an exponential function look like, and why does it always increase or always decrease (never both)?
faqs.answer:
For \( f(x) = b^x \) with \( b > 0 \) and \( b \ne 1 \), the graph is a smooth curve that is either always climbing (growth, when b > 1) or always falling (decay, when 0 < b < 1), never both on the same graph. (If b = 1, the graph is the flat line y = 1, which is why b = 1 is not allowed.) This is because multiplying by the same factor b every step can only push the output consistently up or consistently down; there's no mechanism for the curve to turn around and reverse direction like a parabola does.

\( f(x) = 2^x \) always climbs — there's no turning point, unlike a parabola.

faqs.question: What is a horizontal asymptote, and why does \( f(x) = b^x \) have one at y = 0?
faqs.answer:
A horizontal asymptote is a horizontal line that a graph gets closer and closer to as x heads far to the left or far to the right. (Some functions, like certain rational functions, cross their horizontal asymptote somewhere in the middle; an exponential function never does.) For \( f(x) = b^x \) with \( b > 1 \), the outputs get closer and closer to 0 as x becomes very negative; for \( 0 < b < 1 \), such as \( \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^x \), they get closer to 0 as x becomes very large. Either way, b raised to any real power is positive, never exactly 0. That's the asymptote behavior: the curve hugs the line y = 0 on one side without ever reaching it.

The curve hugs y = 0 on the left forever, but never quite touches it.

faqs.question: Why does an exponential function never have a vertical asymptote?
faqs.answer: A vertical asymptote is an x-value where the outputs grow without bound as the inputs get close to it. Exponential functions never do that: they are continuous and finite at every real input. As x approaches any finite number a, \( b^x \) approaches the finite value \( b^a \), so there is no vertical asymptote. (In PR7, rational functions had vertical asymptotes at some zeros of the denominator, where the outputs blow up; nothing like that happens with \( b^x \).)

faqs.question: What is the domain and range of the parent exponential function \( f(x) = b^x \)?
faqs.answer: For \( f(x) = b^x \) with \( b > 0 \) and \( b \ne 1 \), the domain is all real numbers, \( (-\infty, \infty) \): you can raise a positive base to any power. The range is \( (0, \infty) \): a positive base raised to any power is positive, so the output is never 0 or negative, but it can get as close to 0 as you like and as large as you like. That is why the graph has the horizontal asymptote y = 0.

faqs.question: What are the y-intercept and x-intercept of the parent exponential function, and why is there no x-intercept?
faqs.answer: For the parent function \( f(x) = b^x \) (with \( b > 0,\ b \ne 1 \)), the y-intercept is (0, 1), since any positive base raised to the power 0 equals 1. There is no x-intercept, because an x-intercept needs an output of exactly 0, and \( b^x \) is always positive: its range is \( (0, \infty) \) (see the FAQ on domain and range above). Transformed exponential functions are different: a shift up or down can create an x-intercept. For example, \( y = -2^x + 4 \) crosses the x-axis at (2, 0).

faqs.question: How do transformations from FN4 apply to graphing exponential functions?
faqs.answer: The transformation rules from FN4 (vertical shift, horizontal shift, reflection across the x-axis, and reflection across the y-axis) apply to exponential functions exactly as they did to any other function. The new part is tracking what each transformation does to the asymptote and the range (see the next four FAQs). The EL2 CheckIt exercise uses shifts and both reflections; a reflection across the y-axis shows up as a base between 0 and 1, like \( \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^x \). Extension (beyond the EL2 CheckIt exercise): stretches and compressions from FN4 also apply, and a vertical stretch alone does not move the asymptote y = 0.

faqs.question: How does a vertical shift affect the asymptote, domain, and range of an exponential function?
faqs.answer:
A vertical shift moves the asymptote by exactly the same amount as the shift, since the whole graph — including the line it hugs — moves together. The domain stays all real numbers, but the range shifts along with the asymptote.

Shifting up 2 moves the whole graph AND its asymptote up 2 — range becomes (2, ∞). The lower curve crosses the dashed line y = 2 because that line is the asymptote of g only, not of f.

faqs.question: How does a horizontal shift affect the asymptote, domain, and range of an exponential function?
faqs.answer: A horizontal shift doesn't touch the asymptote, domain, or range at all — since the asymptote y = 0 is a horizontal line, sliding the graph left or right doesn't change its height. The graph just slides sideways along that same unchanged horizontal boundary. Every point slides left or right, so the y-intercept changes too; the asymptote, domain, and range stay the same.

faqs.question: How does a vertical reflection affect the range of an exponential function?
faqs.answer: A vertical reflection (\( g(x) = -b^x \)) flips the entire graph upside down across the x-axis, which flips the range from positive to negative: instead of (0, ∞), the range becomes (−∞, 0). The asymptote stays at y = 0 either way, since reflecting a line that sits exactly on the x-axis doesn't move it. If a number is also added or subtracted outside, as in \( g(x) = -b^x + k \), flip first and then shift: the asymptote moves to y = k and the curve stays below it, so the range is \( (-\infty, k) \). For example, \( -2^x + 5 \) has asymptote y = 5 and range \( (-\infty, 5) \).

faqs.question: How does a horizontal reflection affect the appearance of growth versus decay?
faqs.answer:
A horizontal reflection (\( h(x) = b^{-x} \)) flips the graph left-to-right, which visually swaps how the graph looks: a growth-shaped curve (b > 1) reflected horizontally looks exactly like a decay curve, and vice versa. The asymptote, domain, and range are all unaffected, since none of those depend on horizontal direction. CheckIt writes this as \( \left(\tfrac{1}{b}\right)^x \), since \( b^{-x} = \left(\tfrac{1}{b}\right)^x \).

Mirror images of each other across the y-axis — same asymptote, same range, opposite direction.

faqs.question: How do I find the domain, range, and asymptote of a transformed exponential function like \( \left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^x + 3 \) or \( -5^x + 2 \)?
faqs.answer:
The domain is always \( (-\infty,\infty) \): shifts and reflections never remove an input from an exponential function. For the asymptote, look at the number added or subtracted outside the exponential, after any minus sign in front has been applied: the asymptote is y = that number, or y = 0 if there is none. A shift inside the exponent, a base between 0 and 1, and a minus sign in front do not move it. Then decide which side the curve is on: with a minus sign in front of the exponential, the curve lies below the asymptote and the range is \( (-\infty, k) \); otherwise it lies above and the range is \( (k, \infty) \). (Careful: \( -(2^x + 3) \) is \( -2^x - 3 \), with asymptote y = −3.) Extension (beyond the EL2 CheckIt exercise): a vertical stretch, as in \( 3 \cdot 2^x + 1 \), does not move the asymptote either.
Worked Examples

\( g(x) = \left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^x + 3 \): shift up 3 → asymptote \( y=3 \), curve above, range \( (3,\infty) \), domain \( (-\infty,\infty) \). (Note \( \left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^x = 4^{-x} \).)

\( h(x) = -5^x + 2 \): flip, then shift up 2 → asymptote \( y=2 \), curve below, range \( (-\infty,2) \), domain \( (-\infty,\infty) \)

\( k(x) = -6^{x-3} \): shift right 3 and flip, nothing added outside → asymptote \( y=0 \), range \( (-\infty,0) \), domain \( (-\infty,\infty) \)

faqs.question: How do I graph a transformed exponential function without plotting a full table of points?
faqs.answer: Start with two anchors: the asymptote (draw it dashed first) and the point where the exponent is 0, which is (0, 1) on the parent graph. Move both with the transformations: a number outside moves the asymptote and the point up or down, a minus sign in front flips the point below the asymptote, and a shift inside the exponent slides the point left or right (so it may no longer be the y-intercept). Then plot one more point one step away: x = 1 more for \( -b^x \pm k \) and \( -b^{x \pm h} \), or x = −1 for \( \left(\tfrac{1}{b}\right)^x \pm k \). Sketch a curve through both points that hugs the asymptote on one end and never crosses it. Example: for \( -3^{x-2} \), the asymptote is y = 0, and the points are (2, −1) and (3, −3).

faqs.question: How does this section connect to FN4 and to EL1?
faqs.answer: This section is really FN4's transformation rules and EL1's exponential function definition, combined. EL1 gave you the algebraic rule (\( f(x) = ab^x \)) and taught you to evaluate it; FN4 gave you the general transformation toolkit (shifts, reflections, stretches); this section applies FN4's toolkit specifically to EL1's function family, with one exponential-specific twist: tracking what happens to the asymptote alongside the domain and range.

faqs.question: Why do asymptotes matter beyond exponential functions?
faqs.answer: Horizontal asymptotes describe what a function approaches as its input grows very large or very negative. Vertical asymptotes describe unbounded behavior near a particular input. That idea runs through the rest of precalculus and into calculus, where it becomes the idea of a limit. You met asymptotes with rational functions in PR7, where a graph can have vertical asymptotes (at some zeros of the denominator) and a horizontal asymptote that the graph may even cross. Exponential functions are the clean case: exactly one horizontal asymptote, approached on one side only, never crossed, and no vertical asymptote. The same pattern shows up again for logarithms, where the asymptote turns vertical.

guided.title: Understand Why the Asymptote Exists
guided.prompt: I'm working on EL2, graphs of exponential functions. My notes say: a horizontal asymptote is a horizontal line the graph gets closer and closer to as x goes far to the left or far to the right; for y = b^x with b > 0 and b ≠ 1, it is y = 0, the domain is all real numbers, and the range is (0, infinity). Before you explain anything, ask me to make a table of 2^x and (1/2)^x for x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, and to tell you for each one on which side (left or right) the outputs get close to 0, and whether any output ever equals 0 or is negative. Ask me why. If I'm stuck, give me a hint as a question, not the answer. Then write a short explanation (3 or 4 sentences) of why y = (1/4)^x - 3 has the asymptote y = -3 and the range (-3, infinity), and put one deliberate mistake in it (for example, saying the curve levels off on the left, putting a bracket at -3, or putting the curve below the asymptote). I'll find the mistake and check it against a table I make myself. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Tracking the Asymptote Through Transformations
guided.prompt: I'm practicing EL2 for my CheckIt: the domain, range, and horizontal asymptote of a transformed exponential function. My notes say: the number added or subtracted outside the exponential sets the asymptote; with a minus sign in front, the curve is below the asymptote and the range is (-infinity, k); otherwise the curve is above it and the range is (k, infinity); a shift inside the exponent moves the graph left or right but not the asymptote; and the domain is always (-infinity, infinity). Give me one function at a time, only in these CheckIt forms: (1/b)^x + k, (1/b)^x - k, -b^x + k, -b^x - k, -b^(x + h), -b^(x - h), where b is 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or e and the shift is a whole number from 2 to 6 that is different from b. For each one I'll give the asymptote first, then the range and domain, and say how I knew. Don't confirm my answer until I've explained it. Mix the forms, and include at least one -b^(x + h) or -b^(x - h). After I've done four, pretend you're a classmate and answer three new ones from the same forms, getting exactly one wrong in a realistic way that fits that function (for example, using the number in the exponent as the asymptote for a -b^(x + h) or -b^(x - h) function, writing (k, infinity) for a -b^x + k or -b^x - k function, or putting a bracket at the asymptote). Don't tell me which one is wrong. I'll find it and explain the fix. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Inside the Exponent or Outside? (Contrast Pairs)
guided.prompt: I keep mixing up a number inside the exponent with a number added outside. Give me pairs of functions that differ only in where the number sits, using EL2 CheckIt forms: -b^(x + h) with -b^x + h, or -b^(x - h) with -b^x - h, where b is 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or e and h is a whole number from 2 to 6 that is different from b. For each pair, before I calculate anything, I'll predict the asymptote and range of each function and say which way the graph moved. Then ask me to check one prediction by computing a point: f(-h) for -b^(x + h), f(h) for -b^(x - h), or f(0) for -b^x + h and -b^x - h. Ask me questions instead of correcting me directly. After three pairs, describe both graphs of a new pair in words (asymptote, two points, and whether the curve is above or below the asymptote), with one deliberate mistake in one of the two descriptions. I'll find it by computing a point myself. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Graphing from Key Features
guided.prompt: I'm learning to graph a transformed exponential function the way the EL2 CheckIt asks: draw any asymptote as a dotted line and label at least two points. My notes say: draw the asymptote first; then plot the point where the exponent is 0 and one more point one step away (for (1/b)^x + k or (1/b)^x - k, use x = 0 and x = -1; for -b^x + k or -b^x - k, use x = 0 and x = 1; for -b^(x + h), use x = -h and x = -h + 1; for -b^(x - h), use x = h and x = h + 1); then sketch a curve that hugs the asymptote on one end and never crosses it. Give me one function in one of those forms, with b equal to 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or e and a shift that is a whole number from 2 to 6 and different from b. Ask me for the asymptote, then my two points, then which end of the curve hugs the asymptote and whether the curve is above or below it. Don't tell me the points; if one is wrong, ask me to recompute it. If I upload a photo of my sketch, check those same things. Then do one yourself: for a new function, give the asymptote, two points, and a description of the curve, with one deliberate mistake (for example, a point with the wrong sign, or the curve on the wrong side of the asymptote). I'll find it by computing the points myself. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Connect This to FN4 and EL1
guided.prompt: I've learned function transformations in FN4 and exponential functions in EL1, and now I'm combining them in EL2. My notes say: from FN4, -f(x) reflects across the x-axis, f(x - h) shifts right h, f(x) + k shifts up k, and the reflection comes before the vertical shift; from EL1, y = b^x with b > 0 and b ≠ 1 passes through (0, 1). Before you explain anything, ask me to describe -2^(x - 4) and -2^x - 4 as transformations of f(x) = 2^x, in order, and to say what each transformation does to the point (0, 1) and to the line y = 0. Then ask me the question that connects them: which FN4 transformations can move a horizontal line, and which cannot? Let me answer before you add anything. Then write a short paragraph explaining why (1/5)^x is a reflection of 5^x across the y-axis, with one deliberate mistake in it (for example, calling it a reflection across the x-axis, or saying it changes the range). I'll find the mistake and check it against my notes. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

paths.label: EL2: Graphs of Exponential Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the EL2 check: graphing exponential functions and finding their domain, range, and asymptote. Practice scope: the EL2 CheckIt exercise uses three function types, each shifted by a whole number from 2 to 6: (1/b)^x plus or minus a shift, −b^x plus or minus a shift, and −b^(x + h) or −b^(x − h), with base b = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or e. The parent graphs in the first skill stop are warm-ups, not CheckIt forms.

stages.desc: Two quick reminders EL2 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Evaluate powers for a table
stops.target: Evaluate \(b^x\) at small whole-number inputs, including negatives: \(b^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{b}\), \(b^0 = 1\).
stops.reflect: Every exponential \(b^x\) passes through one point no matter what \(b\) is. Which point?

stops.title: Interval notation with infinity
stops.target: Write sets like "all numbers greater than 3" in interval notation: \((3, \infty)\). Use a parenthesis at a number that is not included and always at \(\pm\infty\).
stops.cold: Write in interval notation: (a) all real numbers (b) \(y > 3\) (c) \(y < -2\)
stops.coldPlain: Write in interval notation: (a) all real numbers, (b) y > 3, (c) y < -2.
stops.solution: All real numbers runs from negative infinity to infinity: (-infinity, infinity). y > 3 does not include 3: (3, infinity). y < -2 does not include -2: (-infinity, -2). Infinity always gets a parenthesis.
stops.mistake: Using a bracket, like [3, infinity), when the number itself is not included.
stops.reflect: When do you use a parenthesis instead of a bracket?

stages.desc: Parent graphs first, then each transformation the EL2 check uses: shifts up or down, reflections, and shifts left or right.

stops.title: The parent graphs
stops.target: Graph \(y = b^x\) from a table. If \(b > 1\) it rises; if \(0 < b < 1\) it falls. Either way it passes through \((0, 1)\), never touches the horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\), has domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), and range \((0, \infty)\).
stops.cold: Make a table and graph \(y = 2^x\). State the domain, range, and asymptote.
stops.coldPlain: Make a table and graph y = 2^x. State the domain, range, and asymptote.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the asymptote, two labeled points, and whether the graph rises or falls. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Domain \((-\infty, \infty)\). Range \((0, \infty)\). Asymptote \(y = 0\). Each row of the table is a point; the values get close to 0 on the left but never reach it.[[graph:P2]]
stops.solution: Table: (-2, 1/4), (-1, 1/2), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 8). Plot and connect. Going left, the y-values halve forever and approach 0 without reaching it, so y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote and the range is (0, infinity). Every real x works, so the domain is all real numbers.
stops.mistake: Letting the graph touch or cross y = 0, or writing the range with a bracket, [0, infinity).
stops.againA: It falls from left to right. Same domain, range \((0, \infty)\), and asymptote \(y = 0\), now approached on the right.[[graph:P3]]
stops.reflect: Why can \(b^x\) never equal 0 or be negative?

stops.title: Shift up or down: the asymptote moves
stops.target: For \(y = b^x + k\), every point moves up \(k\) (down if \(k\) is negative), including the asymptote: it becomes \(y = k\). With no minus sign in front, the curve stays above it, so the range is \((k, \infty)\).
stops.cold: For \(y = \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^x + 4\), find the domain, range, and asymptote, and graph it.
stops.coldPlain: For y = (1/3)^x + 4, find the domain, range, and asymptote, and graph it.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the asymptote, two labeled points, and whether the graph rises or falls. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Domain \((-\infty, \infty)\). Range \((4, \infty)\). Asymptote \(y = 4\). Add 4 to every \(y\) in the \(\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^x\) table from the last stop.[[graph:A1]]
stops.solution: Adding 4 lifts every point up 4, including the asymptote: y = 0 becomes y = 4. At x = 0: 1 + 4 = 5. At x = -1: 3 + 4 = 7. The graph falls toward y = 4 on the right and stays above it, so the range is (4, infinity). The domain is unchanged: all real numbers.
stops.mistake: Keeping the asymptote at y = 0 after a vertical shift.
stops.again: For \(y = \left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^x - 2\), find the range and asymptote, and graph it.
stops.reflect: Where does the number added at the end show up in the answer?

stops.title: Reflect across the x-axis: the range flips
stops.target: For \(y = -b^x + k\), the graph is flipped below its asymptote \(y = k\), so the range becomes \((-\infty, k)\).
stops.cold: For \(y = -3^x - 4\), find the range and asymptote, and graph it.
stops.coldPlain: For y = -3^x - 4, find the range and asymptote, and graph it.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the asymptote, two labeled points, and whether the graph rises or falls. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Range \((-\infty, -4)\). Asymptote \(y = -4\). Change the sign of every \(y\) in the \(3^x\) table, then subtract 4. Note: \(-3^x\) means \(-(3^x)\), not \((-3)^x\).[[graph:R1]]
stops.solution: -3^x = -(3^x), so first flip: every output of 3^x changes sign and the graph sits below y = 0. Then subtract 4: everything moves down 4, including the asymptote, so it becomes y = -4. At x = 0: -1 - 4 = -5. At x = 1: -3 - 4 = -7. The curve approaches y = -4 on the left, from below: range (-infinity, -4).
stops.mistake: Writing the range as (-4, infinity) out of habit, or reading -3^x as (-3)^x (the negative is outside the power).
stops.again: For \(y = -2^x + 4\), find the range and asymptote, and graph it.
stops.againA: Range \((-\infty, 4)\). Asymptote \(y = 4\). The graph sits below the asymptote.[[graph:R2]]
stops.reflect: How do you know whether the graph is above or below its asymptote?

stops.title: Shift left or right: the asymptote stays
stops.target: A number added to \(x\) inside the exponent slides the graph sideways: \(y = -b^{(x - h)}\) slides \(y = -b^x\) right \(h\), and \(y = -b^{(x + h)}\) slides it left \(h\). The asymptote stays \(y = 0\). The key point \((0, -1)\) moves to where the exponent is 0: \((h, -1)\) for a shift right, \((-h, -1)\) for a shift left.
stops.cold: Graph \(y = -2^{x + 4}\) and state its range and asymptote.
stops.coldPlain: Graph y = -2^(x + 4) and state its range and asymptote.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the asymptote, two labeled points, and whether the graph rises or falls. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Shift left 4, reflected. Range \((-\infty, 0)\), asymptote \(y = 0\). The exponent is 0 at \(x = -4\), giving the point \((-4, -1)\).[[graph:H1]]
stops.solution: The exponent x + 4 equals 0 when x = -4, so the point (0, -1) of -2^x moves to (-4, -1). Next point: x = -3 gives -2^1 = -2. A horizontal shift does not move a horizontal line, so the asymptote is still y = 0, and the reflection keeps every output below it: range (-infinity, 0).
stops.mistake: Moving the asymptote for a left or right shift.
stops.again: Graph \(y = -3^{x - 2}\) and state its range and asymptote.
stops.againA: Shift right 2. Range \((-\infty, 0)\), asymptote \(y = 0\). Key points \((2, -1)\) and \((3, -3)\).[[graph:H2]]
stops.reflect: Which transformations move the asymptote, and which do not?

stops.title: Graph, label, and state everything
stops.target: Put it all together: find the asymptote first (dashed line), then two labeled points, then the domain and range.
stops.cold: Graph \(y = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^x + 3\). Label two points and draw the asymptote as a dashed (dotted) line. State the domain and range.
stops.coldPlain: Graph y = (1/2)^x + 3. Label two points and draw the asymptote as a dashed (dotted) line. State the domain and range.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the asymptote, two labeled points, and whether the graph rises or falls. Check my graph.
stops.solution: The + 3 puts the asymptote at y = 3 and the graph above it. At x = 0: 1 + 3 = 4. At x = -1: 2 + 3 = 5. The graph falls toward y = 3 on the right. Range (3, infinity).
stops.mistake: Plotting (0, 1) out of habit; the + 3 moves it to (0, 4).
stops.again: Graph \(y = -e^x - 2\). Label two points, draw the asymptote, and state the range.
stops.againA: Asymptote \(y = -2\), graph below it. Points \((0, -3)\) and \((1, -e - 2) \approx (1, -4.72)\). Range \((-\infty, -2)\).[[graph:S2]]
stops.reflect: What is the first thing you find when graphing, and why?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same three-part format as the EL2 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: State the domain, range, and asymptote, and graph with two labeled points, the way the EL2 check asks.
stops.cold:
Let \(f(x) = -2^{x - 3}\).
(a) Find the domain and range in interval notation.
(b) Write the equation of any asymptotes.
(c) Graph \(f\). Label at least two points and draw any asymptotes with a dotted line.
stops.coldPlain: Let f(x) = -2^(x - 3). (a) Domain and range in interval notation. (b) Equation of any asymptotes. (c) Graph f with two labeled points and dotted asymptotes.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the asymptote, two labeled points, and whether the graph rises or falls. Check my graph.
stops.solution: (a) Every x works; the reflection puts all outputs below 0: range (-infinity, 0). (b) The shift is horizontal, so the asymptote stays y = 0. (c) The exponent is 0 at x = 3, giving (3, -1); x = 4 gives -2.
stops.mistake: Using a bracket at 0, or shifting the asymptote to y = 3.
stops.again: Let \(f(x) = \left(\tfrac{1}{5}\right)^x - 2\). Find (a) the domain and range, (b) the asymptote, and (c) graph with two labeled points.
stops.stretch: Let \(f(x) = \left(\tfrac{1}{e}\right)^x + 2\). (a) Find the domain and range. (b) Write the equation of any asymptotes. (c) Graph \(f\), labeling at least two points.
stops.stretchA: (a) Domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), range \((2, \infty)\). (b) \(y = 2\). (c) Points \((0, 3)\) and \((-1, e + 2) \approx (-1, 4.72)\). The base \(\tfrac{1}{e}\) is between 0 and 1, so the graph falls and levels off at \(y = 2\) on the right.[[graph:F3]]
stops.reflect: Which part (range, asymptote, or graph) takes you the longest?
